UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                        )
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                         )                                 ER26-3515-000
                                                        )


                     COMMENTS OF DOMINION ENERGY SERVICES, INC.


           Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 1 Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf

of its affiliate, Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia (“Dominion

Energy Virginia”), hereby submits the following comments in the above captioned proceeding

regarding PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) proposal to establish a new supplemental

capacity product, the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”), and related new obligations

deemed necessary to support it.2

           Dominion Energy Virginia, a subsidiary of Dominion Energy, Inc., is a public service

corporation organized under the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia and a public utility subject

to regulation by the Commission and does business in the Commonwealth of Virginia and in the

State of North Carolina. It is a regulated, vertically integrated public utility engaged in the

generation, transmission, distribution, and sale of electric energy. Dominion Energy Virginia

furnishes electric service to approximately 2.8 million retail customers in its approximately 30,000

square miles of certificated service territory covering parts of Virginia and North Carolina. To

provide that service, Dominion Energy Virginia owns and operates a diverse fleet of nuclear, oil,

2

 biomass, pumped storage, hydro, coal, solar, wind and natural gas-fired electric generating

capacity of approximately 21,000 megawatts. Dominion Energy Virginia owns 6,800 miles of

electric transmission lines in Virginia, North Carolina and West Virginia, which is operated by

PJM. Dominion Energy Virginia joined PJM effective May 1, 2005, after obtaining prior approval

from the Commission, the Virginia State Corporation Commission, and the North Carolina Utilities

    I.       Introduction

         The PJM Filing proposes reforms to the PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”)

and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load-Serving Entities in the PJM Region

(“RAA”) to establish IRAS, a load reduction service associated with PJM’s capacity market, that

will be in effect when the capacity market clears short of the PJM Reliability Requirement. 4 New

Large Loads added to the system without matching new capacity will be required to provide IRAS,

i.e., be interruptible at PJM’s direction, during the Delivery Year. To establish IRAS, PJM proposes

several other related changes as part of the framework.

         First, PJM proposes to clarify that Load Serving Entities (“LSE”) interconnecting New

Large Loads in a Delivery Year must bring new capacity in an amount that equals or exceeds the

New Large Loads’ peak load as of the commencement of that Delivery Year. To the extent that

they do not fully cover the peak load, the difference will be considered IRAS eligible and subject

 to reduction requests during Emergencies prior to Pre-Emergency Load Management Response. 5

Second, PJM plans to establish a Large Load Registry to track Large Loads currently on the system

and New Large Loads that will interconnect in the future. The registry will inform load forecasts

and provide information needed to implement IRAS from an eligibility and operational

standpoint.6 Third, PJM defines Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) to establish the

category of new capacity that is required to cover New Large Loads’ peak load and avoid

designation as IRAS for a Delivery Year.7 Fourth, PJM proposes to exclude IRAS eligible load

from the VRR Curve used in the Base Residual Auctions (“BRA”) and Incremental Auctions

(“IA”). By doing so, capacity auction clearing prices will not be influenced by LSE’s that fail to

bring sufficient new capacity online to cover New Large Loads. 8 Finally, PJM proposes a

compensation mechanism for IRAS Large Loads that PJM curtails during a Delivery Year due to

system conditions. PJM requires Electric Distributors to implement the compensation scheme but

will defer to the states and their Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities (“RERRAs”) to

the extent they establish specific retail rates addressing the proposed compensation. 9

         Dominion Energy Virginia generally supports the proposed framework for IRAS.

However, PJM’s approach for implementation as presented in the transmittal letter and the Tariff

amendments raises concerns that it will not accommodate all business models and state regulatory

frameworks within the PJM Region. The following comments highlight where PJM’s proposal

should be further clarified, either through the Commission’s order or a requirement for PJM to

submit a compliance filing.

      II.      Comments

           PJM correctly recognizes that LSEs should have an affirmative obligation to procure new

capacity to cover any new Large Loads they seek to interconnect and serve during a Delivery Year.

LSEs are the wholesale entities serving retail customers, and the costs and obligations for Large

Loads, which are retail customers, should flow through the LSEs. Some of the current resource

adequacy shortfall in PJM can be attributed to the lack of incentives for LSEs to procure new

capacity outside the BRA and LSEs relying solely on the BRA to procure needed new capacity. 10

PJM’s proposed amendment to the RAA to clarify LSE obligations is a needed first step toward

reestablishing resource adequacy obligations.

           Much of PJM’s proposed framework, however, moves needlessly from federal wholesale

jurisdiction into retail jurisdiction and is likely to cause confusion and potential legal challenges.

Instead of establishing IRAS obligations with the LSE, the wholesale jurisdictional entity, PJM

focuses its proposal from the perspective of Large Loads, the retail customer. For example, PJM

chooses to call new capacity eligible to cover New Large Loads, “Bring Your Own New Capacity,”

a term that suggests that the only way for New Large Loads to avoid IRAS is to enter their own

arrangements for new capacity. In describing the BYONC concept, PJM states “to the extent a

New Large Load does not want to provide IRAS, it needs to contract with new capacity that meets


10
  See PJM, Considerations to Better Align Default Service Programs with PJM Capacity Market, February 2026, at
pp. 1 and 11, available at https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-
reports/2026/20260218-considerations-for-default-service-programs-to-better-align-with-pjm-wholesale-
markets.pdf, (“Currently, none of PJM’s seven restructured state procure capacity outside of the capacity market.”
And “Currently, these [restructured] states rely heavily, if not exclusively, on PJM’s capacity market to fulfill their
resource adequacy needs. The capacity market, also known as the Base Residual Auction, was initially intended to
be a truly residual market for states to procure for additional unfilled capacity needs, not to serve as the primary
market to satisfy such needs.”) See also, PJM, Prefiled Statement of Manu Asthana o/b/o PJM Interconnection,
L.L.C. under AD25-7, Docket No. AD25-7-000, at p. 6 (“Load serving entities in some regions appear to be
primarily relying on the spot capacity market rather than using bilateral contracting first, and using the capacity
market as a secondary, residual market. This is exacerbating the affordability challenges referenced above.”)

                                                           4
 the BYONC gating criteria.”11 Proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4 Section VII, titled “Bring Your

Own New Capacity Arrangements with New Large Loads”, is written to only consider

“arrangements” that represent a contractual agreement between a New Large Load and a “resource

owner.” The section places only a reporting obligation on the LSE suggesting that they are not

associated with any BYONC designated to cover the New Large Loads they will serve during the

Delivery Year.12

        This myopic view fails to consider that the regulatory framework for retail electric service

can differ between states and also between LSEs operating within those states. In Virginia, for

example, Vertically Integrated Utilities (“VIU”) like Dominion Energy Virginia have an obligation

to interconnect and serve new customers, including Large Loads, and utilize integrated resource

planning to identify the appropriate build out of new capacity to address resource adequacy needs.

The costs for Dominion Energy Virginia to serve Large Loads are allocated through retail rates

designed to ensure that Large Load customers pay their fair share. There is not an obligation for

Large Loads seeking to interconnect in Dominion Energy Virginia’s franchised territory to either

build or contract for new capacity. In the IRAS framework, Dominion Energy Virginia as LSE

will be the entity arranging for new capacity to cover New Large Load expected to interconnect

during the Delivery Year. New Large Loads “bringing their own new capacity” should not be the

only means to avoid IRAS, as conveyed by the Tariff.

        It is likely that PJM chose its IRAS approach to align the design with the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge13 and to accommodate the regulatory framework in restructured states where

 utilities do not own or build new capacity.14 However, by framing the pathway for avoiding IRAS

based solely on the New Large Load bringing their own new capacity, PJM’s proposal will

assuredly cause confusion in states with VIUs or other utilities that self-supply their capacity

requirements. It also creates a disconnect between the resource adequacy obligation PJM seeks to

place on LSEs in the RAA and the language in the proposed Tariff amendments that place the

obligation solely on New Large Loads.

         If the Commission approves the PJM Filing, it should make clear in its order that IRAS

and BYONC provisions also accommodate Vertically Integrated Utilities and other self-supply

entities that plan generation build out to meet customer load growth in their territories. As PJM

states, there is a need for “regulatory certainty,” but as presented the PJM proposal does not provide

that certainty absent additional clarifications and potentially revised Tariff language. 15 Tariff

amendments would not require any significant change to the proposal itself but would involve

reframing the obligations from the standpoint of the LSE serving the New Large Load.

Attachment A to this filing provides example edits to PJM’s proposed Tariff Attachment DD-4,

Section VII to accomplish this adjusted approach. Additional conforming edits would be required

throughout the Tariff and the RAA.

 /media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260116-pjm-board-letter-re-results-of-the-cifp-

 relationship with LSEs rather than individual retail customers.”)

    III.      Conclusion

          Dominion Energy Virginia respectively requests that the Commission issue an order

granting PJM’s proposed Tariff revisions subject to clarification of the issues discussed above or

subject to a compliance requirement for PJM to submit amended Tariff language reframing the

obligations from the standpoint of the LSE serving New Large Load.



Respectfully submitted,

 VII.    REQUIREMENTS FOR ASSOCIATING BRING YOUR OWN NEW
        CAPACITY ARRANGEMENTS WITH NEW LARGE LOADS

(a)     For any BYONC to be in an arrangement associated with a New Large Load, the Load
        Serving Entity serving the New Large Load or the applicable Electric Distributor shall
        report the BYONC associated with the New Large Load in accordance with the PJM
        Manuals.

        (i) If the BYONC is owned or affiliated with the Load Serving Entity serving the
        New Large Load, the Load Serving Entity must certify to the Office of
        Interconnection, in accordance with the PJM Manuals, attesting that the BYONC
        will follow the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VIII. the Load
        Serving Entity serving the New Large Load or the applicable Electric Distributor
        shall report the BYONC in an arrangement with the New Large Load, in accordance
        with the PJM Manuals. The Office of the Interconnection may also accept
        information to the extent interconnection customers, Large Loads, Transmission
        Owners, or other entities voluntarily report any BYONC that may be in an
        arrangement with a New Large Load; and

        (ii) If the BYONC is not owned by or affiliated with the Load Serving Entity
        serving the New Large Load, the resource owner or entity with contractual authority
        over the BYONC to enter into a BYONC arrangement must certify to the Office of
        Interconnection, in accordance with the PJM Manuals, attesting to the arrangement
        that the BYONC will be associated with the New Large Load and that the BYONC
        will follow the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VIII.

(b) For BYONC associated with an arrangement between a New Large Load and
BYONC to be effective for the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Years, for any
associated BYONC arrangement to be considered, the requirements of Tariff, Attachment
DD-4, section VII(a) must be met by April 1 for the first Delivery Year such arrangement
association is to result in a reduction in the New Large Load’s Eligible New Large Load
Amount. By April 15, the Office of the Interconnection shall update the Large Load
Registry to reflect any verified arrangements associations between New Large Loads and
BYONC.

(c) For BYONC associated with an arrangement between a New Large Load and BYONC
to be effective for the 2029/2030 Delivery Year, for any associated BYONC arrangement
to be considered, the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(a) must be
reported to the Office of the Interconnection no later than by 50 days prior to the
commencement of the 2029/2030 Base Residual Auction or by 30 days prior to the posting
of the planning parameters for the Incremental Auctions arrangement for the 2029/2030
Delivery Year. The Office of the Interconnection shall update the Large Load Registry to
reflect any verified arrangements associations between New Large Loads and BYONC
after the relevant RPM Auction.

(d)    For BYONC associated with an arrangement between a New Large Load and

                                             9
 BYONC to be effective for the 2030/2031 Delivery Year and subsequent Delivery Years,
the requirements of Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(a) must be reported to the Office
of the Interconnection no later than by 30 days prior to the posting of the planning
parameters for the relevant RPM Auction for the initial Delivery Year the BYONC enters
into an arrangement with the New Large Load. The Office of the Interconnection shall
update the Large Load Registry to reflect any verified arrangements associations between
New Large Loads and BYONC after the relevant RPM Auction.

(e) BYONC that is in an arrangement associated with a New Large Load must remain in
such arrangement associated with that New Large Load unless and until the New Large
Load is permanently out-of-service.

(f) A physical resource may support multiple BYONC, each of which may be in an
arrangement associated with different New Large Loads, as long as no BYONC is in an
arrangement associated with more than one New Large Load.

(g)    A Load Serving Entity may associate New Large Load may enter into an
arrangement with discrete BYONC supported by different physical resources.

(h) A Load Serving Entity may associate New Large Load may enter into an arrangement
with BYONC in excess of its current Eligible Large Load Amount, e.g., to allow for
expected growth in the New Large Load, and the full megawatt quantity of such BYONC
shall be offered in the first RPM Auction for which the New Large Load is included in the
Variable Resource Requirement Curve,.

       (i) For any generation or storage resource, the Accredited UCAP of any BYONC
       shall be the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which the BYONC cleared
       for the initial Delivery Year the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large
       Load.

       (ii)    For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources, the
       Accredited UCAP shall be the Accredited UCAP for the RPM Auction in which
       the BYONC cleared for the initial Delivery Year the BYONC is in an arrangement
       with the New Large Load and must be demonstrated each year for a 10-year period
       using the Demand Response or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources installed
       capacity for the first Delivery Year after the BYONC is in an arrangement with the
       New Large Load. For Demand Resources or DER Capacity Aggregation Resources
       that are also the actual New Large Load, there is no demonstration required for the
       initial Delivery Year only to not be an Eligible New Large Load.
